episode.observableAction: On a clear midafternoon in a science classroom at the regional school, the subject stands at a black-topped lab table with a shallow plastic tray of water, a small stack of paper clips, and a printed worksheet that states, “Objects denser than water always sink.” The teacher has just finished giving general instructions and moves to another group, leaving the subject working alone at their station. episode.observableAction: On a mild early evening at the home, the subject and the younger sibling sit side by side at the small kitchen table with a worn deck of standard playing cards and a folded sheet of paper listing several game names in the sibling’s handwriting. The sibling looks at the list for a few seconds, circles “Crazy Eights” with the pencil, and says they want that one. The subject nods, gathers the cards into a neat stack, shuffles them, and begins dealing while the sibling watches the cards being passed out across the table.

episode.observableAction: On a quiet midafternoon in a classroom at the regional school, the subject sits alone at a desk near the window during a free period with the paperback copy of “Meditations – Marcus Aurelius” open in front of them. episodes.observableAction: In late afternoon light in a modest living room, a six-year-old sits on the floor driving a small plastic truck along couch cushions as a road when a toddler sibling grabs for the same truck, leading to tugging, raised voices, and the caregiver stepping in from the kitchen, placing a hand on the truck, saying they should take turns, and briefly kneeling nearby while the older child drives the truck along the cushion road twice as the younger sibling waits with a hand near the front bumper.

On a breezy late afternoon in the kitchen of the modest home, the seven-year-old stands on a chair pulled up to the counter, holding a small plastic bowl while the caregiver spoons dry beans from a bag into a larger pot on the stove. The caregiver pauses, points to the bag, and asks the child to pick up any beans that have rolled onto the floor so nobody steps on them. The child climbs down, crouches, and moves along the linoleum, sliding scattered beans into their palm and dropping them into the bowl. The toddler sibling toddles in, watches, and kicks one bean farther under a cabinet with a small shoe. The older child lies on their side to reach an arm under the cabinet edge, scrapes the bean out with their fingertips, and adds it to the bowl. When the floor around the stove and chair is clear, the child carries the bowl back to the counter and shows it to the caregiver, who glances at the collected beans and nods before turning back to stir the pot.

On a cool Saturday afternoon in the living room, a nine-year-old sits cross-legged on the carpet coloring the side of a boxy truck on printer paper with short colored-pencil strokes, other half-finished vehicle and house drawings spread beside them, while a younger sibling kneels nearby nudging extra pencils, and a caregiver carrying a laundry basket pauses to look at the scattered drawings, briefly picks up a page with a lopsided house, comments on the tall tree with branches over the roof, then sets the page back, lifts the basket again, and walks toward the bedrooms as the child resumes shading the truck.

On a chilly late afternoon at the cooperative market, the ten-year-old stands just inside the entrance holding a folded shopping list while the caregiver, shrugging off a light jacket, points toward the aisles and says they only need flour, beans, and dish soap and that the child can go get the flour alone. The caregiver walks toward the service counter to speak with the person there, glancing back once. The child walks down the main aisle past stacked crates, pauses at a row of shelves, and scans the bags until spotting the brand written on the list. They lift a medium paper bag of flour from a lower shelf with both hands, steady it against their chest, and carry it carefully back along the aisle, stepping around another shopper’s cart. Reaching the front, they set the bag on the worn checkout counter edge beside the caregiver, unfold the list to show the crossed-off flour line, and wait while the caregiver finishes the brief conversation and nods toward the bag before turning to pay.

On a midafternoon at the modest home’s kitchen table, the eleven-year-old sits with a worn deck of playing cards spread in small piles while their six-year-old sibling stands on a chair beside them, looking between two bright card backs the older child is holding up. The older child says the sibling can only pick one game to play before dinner and taps one card, saying it means the simple matching game, then taps the other, saying it means the longer game with keeping score. The sibling hesitates, glancing toward the hallway, and asks which one takes less time. The older child points to the matching-game card again and says that one will be done faster so they can still watch a show later, then sets both cards face down on the table and slides them a little closer, telling the sibling they can choose. The sibling reaches out, taps the card for the matching game, and the older child nods, gathers the deck, and begins dealing pairs into a grid. As they start turning over the first two cards together, the caregiver walks through carrying a laundry basket, pauses to look at the spread cards, and continues down the hall without interrupting.

On a darkening Saturday evening at the cooperative market, a twelve-year-old stands outside the entrance with a folded twenty-dollar bill and a short handwritten list while their caregiver, turning toward the parking area, reminds them to get milk and dish soap and to bring back the change, then points to the lit doorway and says they will wait in the vehicle; the child walks inside alone, picks up a wire basket, goes to the refrigerated case to take a gallon of the usual brand of milk, then to the cleaning aisle to compare two bottles of dish soap before choosing the smaller one, proceeds to the single open register, places the items on the counter, smooths out the bill and hands it to the shopkeeper, answers quietly when asked about a bag, receives a few bills and coins and a thin paper receipt, tucks the change and receipt into a front pocket, and carries the milk by its handle and the soap in the other hand back through the sliding door toward the idling family vehicle in the dim lot.

On a chilly early evening at the cooperative market, a thirteen-year-old walks up alone from the direction of the bus stop, pushes open the glass door, and steps inside holding a short list and a folded bill. Without anyone accompanying them, they take a wire basket from the stack, move through the aisles to pick out a bag of flour, a sack of beans, and a small bottle of dish soap, pausing once to check the list and compare two brands of beans before choosing the one written down. They carry the basket to the single open register, set the items on the counter, answer the shopkeeper’s brief question about needing a bag, hand over the bill, wait while the items are rung up, then take the change and receipt directly into their own pocket. Balancing the bag of flour against one hip and gripping the other items in their free hand, they push back out through the door into the dim parking area and start down the sidewalk toward home without meeting up with any caregiver in the lot.

On a breezy Saturday afternoon at the kitchen table of the modest home, a fifteen-year-old sits with a worn deck of playing cards and two DVD cases laid side by side, one showing a cartoon cover and the other a live-action adventure. Their ten-year-old sibling leans on the opposite chair, saying they can only watch one movie before the caregiver gets home. The older teen taps the cartoon case and says it is shorter, then taps the adventure case and says it is longer but has more action. They slide both cases closer to the sibling and say the sibling has to pick because there is only time for one. The younger child looks from one case to the other, asks again which one will finish before dinner, and the older teen points to the cartoon case and repeats that it will end earlier. After a few seconds, the sibling reaches out, rests a hand on the adventure case, then shifts and firmly taps the cartoon case instead. The fifteen-year-old nods, picks up the cartoon DVD case, sets the other one aside on the counter, and walks with the sibling into the living room, where they kneel by the TV stand together while the older teen opens the chosen case and swaps discs in the player.

On an early Saturday evening in the shared hall, a caregiver and a sixteen-year-old review a mobile-library flyer that notes visits on the teen’s usual market day, then the caregiver goes to the notice board, writes their family name and address on the sign-up sheet beside the announcement, and hands the folded flyer to the teen before they walk together toward the rows of chairs as the projector starts up.

On a cool Saturday late afternoon in the shared hall during a mobile-library stop, a seventeen-year-old stands at a folding table where paperbacks are laid out while their caregiver finishes speaking with the visiting librarian near the door. The teen picks up a thin booklet with a plain cover showing the title and a small cross, flips it open, and reads a short printed passage that begins, "If God is just, then every event has a purpose beyond human understanding." They run a finger under the sentence, glance toward the caregiver, then back at the page and quietly reread the line. After a moment, they close the booklet, set it back in the stack, and move along the table to the next row of books as the caregiver walks over, touches their elbow, and says they have about ten minutes before the bus comes.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: short pamphlet on divine justice

episodes.observableAction: Late afternoon light comes through the living-room window as the subject sits on the floor with colored pencils around a half-finished drawing while a younger sibling crawls nearby batting at a toy car; a red pencil rolls under the couch, the subject searches on hands and knees without finding it, then calls to Caregiver 1, who comes from the kitchen, pulls the couch away from the wall, retrieves the pencil from the exposed strip of carpet along with a sock and a plastic block, hands the pencil to the subject, tosses the other items onto a chair, pushes the couch back, and returns to the kitchen as the subject resumes coloring and the sibling moves to the chair to poke at the block.

On a breezy late afternoon, the subject and younger sibling sit on the living-room rug sharing a plastic bin of building blocks, both grab the same long flat piece while saying different uses for it, the sibling’s pull knocks blocks from the tall tower so it collapses and scatters, the subject shouts, "You broke it!" as they both still hold the piece, and Caregiver 1 comes from the kitchen, takes the piece away to the coffee table, roughly gathers the scattered blocks back into a pile between the children, and returns to the kitchen while they remain on the rug with the remaining pieces.

Late on a windy afternoon, the subject sits at the kitchen table with a sheet of paper covered in pencil sketches of a long bus with big windows, a smaller car, and stick figures standing by a sign, eraser crumbs scattered around. The younger sibling climbs onto the next chair and leans over the table, bumping the subject’s elbow so the pencil makes a dark line across one of the bus windows. The subject pulls the paper closer and says, "Hey, don’t," while the sibling points at the page and says, "That’s me," tapping one of the stick figures. Caregiver 1 walks in from the hallway carrying a folded laundry basket, pauses by the table, and sets the basket on a chair. Looking down at the paper, Caregiver 1 says, "Oh, you drew the bus stop by the market," then taps the drawn car and adds, "Is that our car there?" before picking up the laundry basket again and heading toward the bedrooms as the subject keeps the paper in front of them and the sibling stays standing on the chair, still looking at the drawing.

After dinner on a cool evening, the subject, younger sibling, and Caregiver 1 stand in the small front yard beside the driveway looking at a few bright stars, the sibling points to one and calls it the North Star, Caregiver 1 disagrees and points to a different area of the sky, the subject compares both spots and references the tree and roofline while the sibling repeats what a teacher said, and after a brief exchange Caregiver 1 says it is getting cold and leads everyone back inside.

On a mild Saturday early evening, the subject sits at the kitchen table with a spiral notebook open to a page of pencil sketches showing a row of small houses, a taller building with a sign, and a bus with a door drawn halfway. The younger sibling climbs onto the chair beside them, leans over, and taps the taller building, saying, "That’s the school." The subject shakes their head and says, "No, that’s the market," pointing to the drawn sign above the door. Caregiver 1 walks in from the hallway drying their hands on a dish towel, glances at the page, and says, "That looks like the bus stop by the school to me," tapping the same building the sibling pointed at. The subject points to a smaller rectangle with a shaded front and says, "The school is over here," while the sibling insists, "But the bus stops at school." Caregiver 1 laughs shortly, sets the towel on the counter, and says, "The bus stop is closer to the market than the school," as they move to the sink and turn on the water, leaving the subject and sibling still at the table looking down at the drawing and the different labeled buildings.

On a cool evening, the subject, younger sibling, and Caregiver 1 sit around the kitchen table after dinner with a folded county bus schedule and a school notice about a Saturday activity spread out between them. Caregiver 1 taps the printed time for the morning bus and says, "It leaves at eight from the hub," while sliding a finger along the line of small numbers. The sibling leans over and says, "No, last time it was nine, remember?" pointing to a different row on the schedule. The subject picks up the paper, traces the column under the date of the activity, and says, "It says eight-thirty here," then turns the page to check the return times. Caregiver 1 shakes their head and says, "That’s the weekday schedule; Saturdays are over here," flipping the paper back and tapping another column, while the sibling insists, "But we waited until nine last time." The three of them bend closer over the schedule, comparing the rows and pointing at different times as the kitchen clock ticks above the sink.

On a warm Saturday afternoon, the subject, younger sibling, and Caregiver 1 sit at the kitchen table with a school flyer for an after-school art club and a folded county bus schedule, discuss that the club meets Tuesdays from 4 to 5:30 and conflicts with the regular bus, compare the usual 4:10 departure and a later 5:15 bus, and then Caregiver 1 decides the subject will attend the art club on Tuesdays and be picked up by car while the sibling rides the regular bus home, with plans to inform the bus driver and teacher on Monday.

On a cool Saturday evening at the kitchen table, the subject and younger sibling compare a worn paperback and a school book-order flyer, discuss page length and themes like dragons, and the sibling ultimately marks the dragon book on the flyer while the subject leaves the paperback open between them.

On a breezy Saturday early evening, the subject, younger sibling, and Caregiver 1 sit around the kitchen table with a folded county bus schedule, a printed notice about a new weekend art workshop, and a handwritten list of household errands while they point to different times and notes on the papers, compare Saturday and weekday bus columns, mention past delay from road work and the need to visit the coop market before it closes, and then Caregiver 1 circles the 9:15 Saturday bus time in pen, states they will all leave on that bus and go to the market after the workshop, and pushes the schedule and notice to the center of the table as the sibling nods and the subject sets the pen beside the papers.

On a chilly Saturday early evening in the shared hall, rows of metal chairs face a folding table where a visiting speaker has left a stack of thin paperbacks with a simple cross on the cover and the title "Sermon on the Mount" in plain type. After the talk ends and people begin to stand and stretch, the subject and Caregiver 1 move up the aisle together. A volunteer at the table says, "You can take one if you want to read it," tapping the stack. Caregiver 1 picks up a copy, flips through a few pages of closely spaced text, and hands it to the subject, saying, "This is the part where Jesus talks about loving your enemies and turning the other cheek." The subject looks down at a page where the heading "Blessed are the peacemakers" is printed in bold, runs a finger under one short paragraph, and then tucks the booklet under their arm as they and Caregiver 1 step away from the table toward the exit while other attendees drift past, some taking copies and some walking by without stopping.

rejectedRecord.observableAction: On a gray Saturday afternoon in a multipurpose room at the regional school, the subject sits in a circle of metal chairs with a dozen other students for a youth discussion group advertised on a flyer. A student across the circle, wearing a faded team hoodie, leans forward and says, “I don’t know if voting even matters out here. They never fix the buses or the internet, so what’s the point?” then glances around and adds, “I mean, maybe I’m wrong, but that’s how it feels.” A few students nod or look down at their hands. The subject shifts in their chair, looks briefly at the floor, then raises a hand halfway and says, “I kind of disagree. They changed the bus schedule after people kept complaining at the town meeting, remember? And my aunt says the county board decides that stuff, and they’re elected.” The hoodie-wearing student shrugs and replies, “Yeah, but that took forever, and it was just one route.” The subject keeps their voice steady and says, “Still, if nobody shows up or votes, they can just ignore us. At least if more people vote, they have to listen a little.” A couple of students glance between the two speakers; one shifts uncomfortably and another quietly taps a foot. The room falls silent for a moment until another student changes the subject by asking what age they’ll be able to vote in the next election, and the conversation moves on while the subject leans back in their chair and folds their arms loosely.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: Whether voting and local civic participation matter in improving services like buses and internet in their rural area

episodes.observableAction: In the late afternoon, the subject sits on the living-room floor near a low table, spreading out a small pile of crayons and a partly colored worksheet from school. The younger sibling crawls closer and reaches for the same red crayon the subject is using. Both children grab the crayon at once, their hands overlapping. The subject pulls it toward the worksheet, and the sibling tugs it back toward an empty coloring book page. The crayon bends slightly between them. The caregiver, folding laundry on the couch a few feet away, looks up and says, “You two need to share that one.” The subject loosens their grip just enough for the sibling to yank the crayon free and start scribbling on their own page. The subject watches, then picks up a different color from the scattered pile and resumes coloring the worksheet border while the sibling continues using the red on their book.

On a breezy late afternoon, the subject stands in the small front yard holding a short list while the caregiver unloads grocery bags from a compact car, asks the subject to put cans with paper labels on the bottom shelf, and the subject carries a light plastic bag into the narrow kitchen, kneels to place the cans in a row with labels facing outward, stops a can rolled by a younger sibling and adds it to the row, then hangs the empty bag on a hook and verbally reports completion to the caregiver at the doorway.

On a cool early evening, the subject kneels on the living-room rug near a low coffee table, spreading out colored pencils and a half-finished school worksheet that asks for a drawing in one corner. The younger sibling sits beside them with a blank sheet of printer paper. A single sharp black colored pencil lies between them. The subject reaches for it and begins outlining a shape on the worksheet. The sibling leans in, grabs the other end of the pencil, and pulls, saying they need it to draw on their own page. The pencil jerks sideways, leaving a dark streak across the subject’s paper. Both children tighten their grips and tug in opposite directions, the pencil bowing slightly. The caregiver, passing through the room carrying a folded towel, stops and looks down at their hands, then says, “Hey, one at a time with that pencil. You can trade off or pick another color.” The subject hesitates but keeps hold of the pencil; the sibling lets go with a small huff and reaches into the scattered pile to pick up a blue pencil instead, turning back to their blank page while the subject straightens their worksheet and resumes outlining with the black pencil.

On a bright, cool afternoon, the subject walks with the caregiver into the cooperative market, takes a metal shopping basket, and moves alone through the aisles comparing a short handwritten list with shelf labels, placing a small bag of rice, a jar of peanut butter, a carton of eggs, and a roll of paper towels into the basket before returning to the front counter, where the caregiver checks the items and begins paying while the subject stands nearby with the basket on the floor.

On a chilly midafternoon, the subject and the locally working caregiver sit on metal folding chairs in the shared hall while a visiting extension worker at the front finishes a short seed-planting demonstration, showing how different soil depths affect sprouting. After the group claps and people begin to stand, the caregiver and subject walk up to the front table where small plastic cups of soil and seeds are laid out. The extension worker has just pushed one clear cup aside to show a seed resting near the surface. The subject looks at the cup, then at a laminated diagram taped to the table that shows roots growing straight down, and says to the extension worker, “But if the seed is sideways like that, do the roots still go down?” The extension worker pauses, picks up the cup, tilts it so the subject can see the seed’s position, and starts to answer while the caregiver stands just behind the subject, watching and holding a folded flyer.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: seed orientation and root growth after planting

episodes.observableAction: On a cool early evening, the subject and caregiver enter the cooperative market, where the caregiver hands the subject a short handwritten list and some folded bills before stepping aside to talk with the shopkeeper, and the subject takes a wire basket, moves alone through the aisles checking the list against shelf labels, selects rice, peanut butter, eggs, and paper towels, compares two brands of eggs and chooses the one whose price matches the list, then returns to the counter, places the basket down, unfolds the bills, listens as the shopkeeper states the total, counts out the money, receives change, puts it in a pocket, collects the bagged groceries, walks back to the caregiver, states they are done, and they leave together carrying the bags toward the exit.

On a clear midafternoon in a science classroom at the regional school, the subject stands at a black-topped lab table with a shallow plastic tray of water, a small stack of paper clips, and a printed worksheet that states, “Objects denser than water always sink.” The teacher has just finished giving general instructions and moves to another group, leaving the subject working alone at their station. The subject reads the line on the worksheet, then carefully slides a dry paper clip flat onto the surface of the water using the edge of a small index card. The paper clip stays floating on the surface, supported by surface tension. The subject leans closer, taps the side of the tray lightly with a fingertip, and watches the paper clip continue to float without breaking through. After a few seconds, the subject picks up a pencil and writes a short note in the margin next to the printed claim while glancing toward the front of the room where the teacher is helping another student.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: Claim that objects denser than water always sink

episodes.observableAction: On a mild early evening at the home, the subject and the younger sibling sit side by side at the small kitchen table with a worn deck of standard playing cards and a folded sheet of paper listing several game names in the sibling’s handwriting. The sibling taps a pencil on the paper and says they can’t decide which game to play. The subject picks up the paper, reads down the list—“Go Fish,” “War,” and “Crazy Eights”—and asks the sibling what they feel like, pointing first to “War” and then to “Crazy Eights.” The sibling shrugs and says they don’t know, then asks which one is faster. The subject briefly explains that “War” mostly means flipping cards and that “Crazy Eights” uses choosing cards to match numbers or suits, then pushes the paper back toward the sibling and says they should pick whichever sounds more fun. The sibling looks at the list for a few seconds, circles “Crazy Eights” with the pencil, and says they want that one. The subject nods, gathers the cards into a neat stack, shuffles them, and begins dealing while the sibling watches the cards being passed out across the table.

On a midafternoon in early March, the subject stands in front of a tall metal bookshelf in a quiet corner of the regional school library, looking over a row of paperback books with different colored spines. A laminated sign on the shelf reads “Philosophy / Religion.” The subject slides one book out partway, reads the title on the spine, pushes it back in, then tilts their head to read the neighboring titles. After a few seconds, they hook a finger over the top of a thin volume with a plain white spine and pull it free, revealing a cover that reads “Meditations – Marcus Aurelius” in dark letters. The subject flips the book open near the middle, glances down a page of short numbered paragraphs, then closes it halfway and looks back at the shelf where several other books with more colorful covers remain untouched. Holding the white-spined book in one hand, the subject turns away from the shelf and walks toward an empty table near the window, pulls out a chair, sits, and lays the book flat on the table, opening it again to the first pages while the rest of the shelf remains behind them.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: Meditations by Marcus Aurelius

episodes.observableAction: On a quiet midafternoon in a classroom at the regional school, the subject sits alone at a desk near the window during a free period with the paperback copy of “Meditations – Marcus Aurelius” open in front of them. A loose-leaf notebook lies to the right, opened to a blank page, and a ballpoint pen rests across the top spiral. The subject turns a page in the book, pauses over a short numbered paragraph printed near the top that states, “You have power over your mind — not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength,” then glances toward the front of the empty room where the whiteboard is covered with faint marker residue from an earlier class. After a few seconds, the subject picks up the pen, pulls the notebook a little closer, and copies the sentence onto the blank page, writing the words in a single line. When they finish, they underline the phrase “not outside events,” close the notebook halfway so the written line is still visible, and then look back down at the open book, resting one hand lightly on the page as they continue reading while the room remains quiet around them.

intellectualEncounter.subjectLabel: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (Stoic reflections)
